summary: This informational document describes an experimental use case for autonomic networking: detecting violations of service level agreements in a distributed way. It aims to place and adapt measurement probes automatically for efficient monitoring.

eli5.summary: Network devices team up to check on their own whether the promised service is being delivered, and move their measuring tools to where needed.

questions: how does autonomic networking detect sla violations
subtitle: Self-managing networks that detect when service quality dips

tldr.problem: Services like video streaming or trading require guaranteed performance levels (Service Level Agreements). Monitoring these requires active measurement probes sent from network devices, but placing them optimally requires labor-intensive manual configuration that doesn't adapt quickly to network changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes using autonomic networking, where devices automatically decide which destinations to measure and coordinate with peers, learning from past results which destinations are most critical and adjusting probe placement dynamically without human intervention.
tldr.outcome: Networks can detect violations of performance promises more efficiently and quickly, catching problems while still within budget, without requiring network administrators to constantly reconfigure monitoring.

today: RFC 8316 is an Informational document from the IRTF describing an experimental use case. It represents the consensus of the Network Management Research Group. While not yet a standard, it serves as a reference for research and future standards work in autonomic network management and SLA detection.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Services running on the Internet often operate under Service Level Agreements (SLAs) that promise performance targets such as latency, packet loss, and jitter. These promises are formalized as Service Level Objectives (SLOs). Violations of SLOs can cost users significant money: a trading firm loses on delayed orders, an online retailer loses customers when pages load slowly, a gaming provider loses players to latency.

To protect against violations, service providers need continuous monitoring at the network infrastructure layer. This is traditionally done with active measurements: injecting synthetic test traffic from probes to simulate real application traffic. Unlike passive measurements (which observe real traffic), active measurements offer more control, accuracy, and privacy. However, they consume network resources and CPU on devices, so the number of measurement destinations must be carefully limited.
sections.eli5: Services promise to be fast. To check if they're keeping that promise, networks send test traffic. But the test traffic costs money, so you have to choose wisely where to send it.

sections.title: The Problem with Current Approaches
sections.content:
Today, network administrators manually determine the best locations for measurement probes. They gather traffic information, infer likely destinations for testing, activate measurement sessions on chosen endpoints, and account for available resources. This approach does not scale well: it is labor-intensive, error-prone, and cannot adapt quickly when network conditions change.

In modern data centers, the most critical flows (those that should be measured) change rapidly as virtual machines migrate and new customer demands arrive. Human administrators simply cannot react fast enough to reconfigure probes. As a result, current practice only covers a fraction of network flows, leading to undetected SLA violations—the worst possible outcome.
sections.eli5: Humans have to figure out where to put the monitors. That's slow, tedious, and doesn't keep up when the network changes. As a result, problems get missed.

sections.title: A Distributed Autonomic Solution
sections.content:
The RFC proposes embedding autonomic control in network devices themselves. Each device implements an Autonomic Service Agent (ASA) that monitors service levels locally and decides which measurement sessions to activate based on current and past observations. Devices coordinate with peer devices using a peer-to-peer (P2P) overlay to share measurement results and collectively achieve optimal coverage.

When a device first comes online, it may start with randomly seeded or round-robin measurements. As measurements accumulate, the device learns which destinations are most critical (those close to SLO thresholds need closer monitoring), which observations from peers are correlated with its own (to avoid redundant monitoring), and which routes are most likely to violate their guarantees. The P2P overlay enables each device to make decisions locally and rapidly while benefiting from observations across the network, creating faster adaptation than a centralized controller could achieve.
sections.eli5: Put a smart agent on each device. It learns which destinations need watching and talks to other devices to coordinate. Together, they move the monitors to where violations are most likely.

sections.title: User Experience and Control
sections.content:
An autonomic SLA detection system requires minimal human interaction after deployment. Administrators do not need to plan which measurements to conduct or configure probes and responders. However, they retain important control: they receive notifications and reports of detected violations, and they can set policies for monitoring intensity.

For example, an administrator might specify a resource budget (the maximum number of concurrent measurement sessions or total test traffic allowed) and let the system maximize the number of detected violations within that budget. Alternatively, they might set a detection target (for example, "detect 95% of all violations") and let the system minimize resource consumption to reach that target. The solution adapts automatically to changing network conditions and changes in VM placement without requiring reconfiguration.
sections.eli5: Once you set it up, it runs itself. You just tell it "monitor hard" or "use less traffic," and it figures out the rest. You get reports when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
Implementation requires devices to have self-knowledge about local SLA monitoring, including historical measurement data and SLOs, plus algorithms to select which probes to activate. The solution should leverage existing active measurement protocols like OWAMP (One-Way Active Measurement Protocol) and TWAMP (Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol) for interoperability.

Devices must exchange measurement results to optimize decisions. A topology of management peers (devices that share data) can be built using network neighbors as initial seeds and refined based on correlations in observed data. The Autonomic Control Plane (ACP) provides an ideal secure foundation for the P2P overlay. The solution must handle multiple deployment scenarios, including physical devices and virtualized network functions, and must discover both measurement peers and measurement targets (responders) dynamically.
sections.eli5: Devices need to remember past measurements, run algorithms to pick targets, and talk to each other about what they found. They use standard testing protocols and a secure P2P network to coordinate.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The security of the solution depends critically on the security of the Autonomic Control Plane. If an attacker compromises the ACP, they could report fraudulent measurement results to peers, causing probes to be deployed ineffectively and SLA violations to go undetected. Similarly, if the autonomic function itself is hijacked, an attacker could exhaust resources by generating excessive measurement traffic, depriving the network of bandwidth and devices of CPU.

The RFC also notes that measurements involving synthetic test traffic could be abused if not protected: an attacker could use them as a covert channel or as a vector for denial-of-service attacks. Protection mechanisms and threat modeling are essential, though detailed security protocols are left to future work.
sections.eli5: If someone breaks into the control system, they can trick the monitors or make them waste resources. The network and autonomic functions must be well protected.
